newsitem.title: USA: LIPA bonds are bet against technology - analyst.
newsitem.headline: LIPA bonds are bet against technology - analyst.

text.p: The bonds the Long Island Power Authority proposes to fund a partial takeover of the Long Island Lighting Co is a 35-year bet against technology in an area of dynamic technological change, according to one analyst for utility investors.
In testimony to a New York Assembly Energy Committee hearing, economist Charles Studness said "there is a very real possibility of default sometime during" the 35 year life of the LIPA bonds.

Pointing out 65 to 70 percent of the proposed $7.7 billion debt issue will still be outstanding in 15 to 20 years, Studness told Reuters Tuesday it is "very difficult to quantify the issue" for potential investors.

He told the hearing the borrowed funds will be used to acquire assets LILCO now values at $6.6 billion. It also includes $462.5 million to finance a tax settlement and $155 million for 1998 rebates to ratepayers.

Providing the committee with an overview of his report to bond-buying institutions, Studness said "the economic value of these assets is only $1.5 to $1.8 billion ... (which) must carry about $6 billion of intangibles.
"The issue for investors is whether LIPA is capable of carrying such a burden."
Among the difficulties in understanding the LIPA proposal, Studness told the hearing, is a lack of data.
"Unfortunately, LIPA has not provided estimates of savings it will provide after the tenth year," he said.

Noting the savings it promises during the "first 10 years far exceed our estimates," he said "This suggests that financial engineering techniques have been used to move savings into the initial years at the expense of later years."
Energy Committee Chairman Paul Tonko said Sudness has posed "some very serious questions" about the LIPA proposal.
In particular the assemblyman cited his projections of "dis-savings" after 15 years, calling this "disconcerting."
"Where LIPA rates would be 24 percent below LILCO's initially, they would be 29 percent above LILCO's at the end of 35 years," Suddness projected in last week's testimony.

Comparing LIPA's proposed rates to savings expected from deregulation efforts now underway, he said the authority promises greater initial savings, but by 2008 Long Island rates will be 23 percent higher relative to California -- and 18 percent higher relative to Massachustts -- than they are now.
LIPA spokesman Seth Hulkower said the authority will be issuing a written response to Sudness' testimony Wednesday.
Besides debt costs, he said, LILCO's distribution and customer service costs are almost twice the industry average.

But LIPA's initial transmission budget will be based on proposals in LILCO's 1996 rate case filing the New York Public Service Commission staff criticized and concluded were excessive by 15 percent, Sudness said.
He noted Brooklyn Union Gas Co has agreed to acquire the parts of LILCO not being acquired by LIPA, including its power plants.

He said these old, inefficient plants are under contract to LIPA for 15 years so "it will have the same generating costs as LILCO has had" and savings that could be realized under competition will be deferred for 12 to 15 years.
At the same time, he said, technologies that will enable customers to generate their own power with enough reliability to disconnect from their utility are becoming economical.

In particular Studness noted Unicom Corp's June 3 announcement it will market AlliedSignal Inc's micro-turbine small power plants described by the two companies as competitive with rates charged small commercial customers in the Midwest -- where electricity rates are well below Long Island's.
Meanwhile, New York Consumer Board Chairman Timothy Carey says the fuel cell at Westchester's sewage plant north of New York City is producing power for $0.07 per kilowatt hour.
Sudness noted LIPA has projected initial rates a bit below $0.12 per kilowatt hour.

"LIPA'S rates will be among the highest in the nation if not the highest," he testified, adding it will serve an affluent area. "This profile will make Long Island and early, prime target" for new technology.

"LIPA might then find itself in a position where it must cut costs to retain customers. If it fails to make sufficient cust, it will lose load and risk going into a contracting death spiral." ((-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610.))
